pac_metadata.title: Edo Japan
pac_metadata.description: The 17th century in Japan marks the beginning of the Edo period under the Tokugawa Shogunate. It was characterized by relative peace, a rigid social hierarchy, the growth of urban centers like Edo, and the implementation of isolationist policies (Sakoku).

dwellings.description: Varies by social class. Commoner homes (minka) are typically single-story, made of wood and earth, with thatched or tiled roofs. Samurai residences range from simple houses to larger compounds, often with gardens and surrounding walls. Daimyo residences are extensive estates within castle towns or Edo.

public_structures.description: Gathering places, markets, tea houses, bath houses, local government offices (yakusho). Often simple wooden structures.
key_features: Often located near main roads or rivers

religious_structures.description: Buddhist temples (tera) and Shinto shrines (jinja). Distinctive architectural styles with curved roofs and elaborate carvings. Temples often have large gates (sanmon) and main halls (hondo). Shrines have torii gates marking the entrance.

construction_techniques_and_materials.description: Dominance of wood (cypress, cedar) and bamboo. Post-and-beam construction. Flexible joinery to withstand earthquakes. Walls made of plaster, wood, or earth. Roofs thatched or tiled (kawara). Paper (washi) for screens and windows. Stone for foundations and castle walls.

everyday_clothing.description: The basic garment for all classes and genders was the kimono or kosode, a T-shaped robe tied with a sash (obi). Style, fabric, and decoration varied greatly by status and occasion.
male_items: Kosode (worn underneath or as casual wear)
Hakama (pleated trousers/skirt, for samurai and formal wear)
female_items: Obi (wider and more decorative than men's)

ceremonial_special_occasion.description: More formal kimono styles (e.g., montsuki with family crests), layered robes (historically from court), Samurai armor (for ceremony, less for daily wear in peace), Wedding attire (shiro-muku, uchikake for brides).
key_features: Specific patterns or colors for rituals

status_indicators_in_clothing.description: Class was clearly indicated by fabric quality, color, pattern size and complexity, and items carried (like swords for samurai). Sumptuary laws dictated what different classes could wear.
indicators: Presence and style of family crests (mon)
Complexity of pattern and dyeing method

weapons_and_armor.description: Samurai weapons primarily swords (katana, wakizashi), yari (spears), and yumi (bows). Firearms (tanegashima) existed but were less central than in the Sengoku period. Armor (yoroi) was used for battle or ceremony.

tools_for_work_and_daily_life.description: Varied by occupation. Farming tools (hoes, sickles, plows, spades), carpentry tools (saws, chisels, planes), weaving looms, pottery wheels, fishing nets and poles, kitchen knives, grinding stones, writing brushes and inkstones.

household_items.description: Items for eating, cooking, sleeping, and daily living. Often made of wood, bamboo, lacquerware, and ceramics.

transportation_methods.description: Primarily walking. Horses were used by samurai and officials. Palanquins (kago) were used for transporting people, especially wealthy or important figures. Boats and ships were crucial for travel along coasts and rivers, and for goods transport.

major_art_styles.description: Key painting schools included Kanō (official, often large-scale, ink/color), Tosa (classical themes, narrative, bright colors), Rinpa (decorative, nature motifs, gold/silver leaf), and the beginnings of Ukiyo-e (woodblock prints and paintings of 'floating world' - courtesans, actors, daily life).

common_motifs_and_symbols.description: Nature was a primary source of inspiration, stylized and symbolic. Animals and mythical creatures also featured.
motifs: Everyday life (chōnin culture, theatre, pleasure quarters in Ukiyo-e)

materials_and_methods_for_artistic_expre.description: Painting on silk or paper (scrolls, screens, fans) using ink (sumi) and mineral pigments. Woodblock printing (mokuhanga) for Ukiyo-e. Lacquering on wood. Ceramics painting. Metalwork.

imagery: Beautiful women (bijin - esp. courtesans in Ukiyo-e)

natural_colors_available.description: Colors derived from plants, minerals, and earth.

dyes_and_pigments_used.description: Techniques for creating dyes and pigments were highly developed.

status_related_color_associations.description: Sumptuary laws often regulated colors. Certain colors or combinations were associated with specific ranks or classes.
associations: Purple (murasaki) often associated with high rank or luxury
Bright colors became popular with the merchant class (sometimes restricted)
Restrained colors like browns, greys, deep blues/greens for samurai and upper classes (often dictated by subtle taste or sumptuary laws)

social_classes_and_their_roles.description: A rigid four-tier system (Shi-Nō-Kō-Shō): Samurai (warriors, administrators - ruling class), Peasants (farmers - primary producers, largest class), Artisans (craftsmen), Merchants (traders, distributors). Below these were outcasts (eta, hinin).

gender_roles_and_responsibilities.description: Patriarchal society. Men were heads of households and primary public figures. Women managed domestic affairs; their specific roles varied greatly by class. Samurai women maintained household honor, merchant women might participate in business, peasant women worked in fields. Women had limited legal rights.
roles: Men: Household head, provider, public representative, warrior (samurai)
Women: Household manager, child-rearing, domestic work, assistance in family trade/farm (varying by class)

family_structure_and_kinship.description: The 'ie' (household) was the fundamental social unit, prioritizing the continuity and prosperity of the household over individuals. Typically multi-generational. Head of household (usually the eldest male) had considerable authority. Inheritance often followed primogeniture.

leadership_and_power_structures.description: The Shogun (military dictator) ruled through the Bakufu (Shogunate) in Edo. Below the Shogun were the Daimyo (feudal lords) who controlled domains. Samurai served the Shogun or Daimyo, forming the administrative backbone. The Emperor in Kyoto held symbolic authority.

typical_daily_routines.description: Routines varied by class and occupation. Generally, days started early, focused on work (farming, craft, trade, official duties). Meals were communal within the household. Evenings involved simple activities or limited entertainment before an early bedtime.
routines: Evening leisure (storytelling, family time, limited outside entertainment)

food_and_diet.description: Rice was the staple for most, though peasants often ate millet or barley. Diet included vegetables (radishes, greens, beans), fermented foods (miso, soy sauce, pickles), fish (fresh and saltwater), tofu. Meat consumption was rare (Buddhist influence). Tea was a common drink; sake (rice wine) was consumed.
diet: Fish (grilled, raw - early forms of sushi)

occupations_and_labor.description: The majority were farmers cultivating rice and other crops. Others were artisans (potters, weavers, carpenters, blacksmiths), merchants (shopkeepers, traders), samurai administrators, laborers, fishermen.

family_life_and_childrearing.description: Centered around the 'ie' (household). Duty to the family head and household was paramount. Children were raised to understand their social status and future role. Education varied; basic literacy was increasing, especially for samurai and merchants.

religious_or_spiritual_practices.description: A mix of Buddhism and Shinto, often practiced alongside each other. Ancestor worship was significant. Visiting temples and shrines for prayer, blessings, and participation in festivals (matsuri). Tea ceremony (Chanoyu) was a formalized spiritual and social ritual.

birth_coming_of_age_marriage_and_death_c.description: Life cycle events were marked by specific rituals, often combining Buddhist and Shinto elements.

customs.birth: Naming ceremonies, visiting shrines (e.g., for protection)
customs.coming_of_age: Genpuku (boys, around 15, receiving adult name and first samurai dress/haircut if applicable), Mogi (girls, receiving adult kimono and hairstyle)
customs.marriage: Formal negotiation between families, exchange of gifts, ceremony (often Shinto or domestic), exchange of sake (san-san-kudo)
customs.death: Buddhist funeral rites most common, mourning periods, memorial services at specific intervals (e.g., 49th day, anniversaries), ancestor tablets in household altars (butsudan)

seasonal_celebrations_and_festivals.description: Festivals tied to the agricultural calendar, seasonal changes, and specific deities/events. Often involved processions, music, special foods, and visits to shrines/temples.
celebrations: Tango no Sekku / Kodomo no Hi (Boys' Day - May 5)

important_ceremonies.description: Official ceremonies related to the Shogunate and court, as well as religious ceremonies.
ceremonies: Official appointments and audiences at Edo Castle
Temple and shrine consecrations and rituals

games_and_sports.description: Board games were popular indoor activities. Physical contests existed but were less emphasized than in the warring states period.

music_and_instruments.description: Music was integral to theatre, festivals, and social gatherings. Instruments included strings, wind, and percussion.
music_instruments: Shamisen (3-stringed lute - popular in urban centers, geisha, theatre)

storytelling_traditions.description: Oral traditions were strong, evolving into formalized performance styles.
traditions: Recitation of classic literature and folk tales

other_leisure_activities.description: Various activities for relaxation and enjoyment, particularly flourishing in urban centers.

behavioral_expectations.description: Strict adherence to social hierarchy and etiquette (reigi). Politeness, humility, respect for elders and superiors. Group harmony over individual desire. Maintaining composure.

taboos_and_forbidden_activities.description: Actions that disrupted social order or violated moral codes.
taboos: Disloyalty to one's lord or family
Unauthorized travel or emigration (due to Sakoku)

honor_and_shame_concepts.description: Central to the samurai code (Bushido) but influenced all classes. Honor was maintained through fulfilling one's duty, loyalty, and courage. Shame resulted from failure, cowardice, or disrespect. Seppuku (ritual suicide) was a way for samurai to regain lost honor.
concepts: Shame as a powerful social force

hospitality_customs.description: Important, especially in rural areas and within formal social contexts like the tea ceremony. Offering tea, refreshments, or meals to guests. Providing shelter to travelers (though inns became more common).
customs: Offering tea and refreshments to guests
